raw_text: {"anchor":"day's business and bodily pain","spark":"great thaw and meeting at Mr. Povy's","wound":"great deal of pain","fuel":null,"bridge":null,"echo":null,"narrative":"After a great thaw, he took coach to Mr. Povy's, where they agreed on an answer to the Lords, and then went to Exeter House. There a witness was furiously angry because another man foolishly said the L26,000 was my Lord Peterborough's account; the Lords found fault with their answer, and he thinks Lord Ashly would fain have the outside of an Exchequer. He went home by coach with Lord Barkeley, who seems to look on Mr. Coventry as an enemy, then sat at the office until evening, supped and went to bed. parsed.narrative: He went to the Duke of Albemarle's and then to Whitehall for a Tangier committee, where new disorder about Mr. Povy's accounts made him think he would never be settled in his business as treasurer. Captain Cooke met him and seemed discontented that his boy Tom had no time for singing or lute, which he answered fully. After dining at the Old James with Sir W. Rider, Cutler and Mr. Deering about hemp, he went to Whitehall to attend the King and Lord Chancellor about navy debts and money, but the meeting failed. Hickes's run-down house, finding the house and the meanest dinner worse than any he had ever seen, and was pleased only by a fine Van Dyck picture of the Queene-Mother. Returning home, he walked with Mr. Pen, who told ill-told observations of France, and found his wife had been out all day, which troubled him as it was late and cold. He went to supper at Pen's mother's, where his wife and Mercer arrived later after being with Captain Cocke, and he had no stomach to eat. After supper he and Mr. Pen argued for an hour or more over the sense of a French song phrase, almost angry and unsatisfied, before going home to bed.

Pen's, he went back to the Prince, spoke with my Lord about trusting Cocke, then took a wherry toward Chatham, where in the dark the ignorant waterman made them go back and forth, which vexed them mightily. A fisher boy guided them safely, and they marvelled at the sea-water seeming like fire at every oar stroke; at the Crowne Inne in Rochester they made merry with the boy, who said he had not been in a bed in seven years of apprenticeship, and then went to bed in their clothes.

He spent the afternoon on a song he had set, then walked with his wife and Mercer to Mrs. Pierce's, where a company met for music and Mr. Pierce unexpectedly arrived from Oxford. He called it the best company for music he had ever been in, wished he could live and die in it, and spent the night almost in ecstasy, especially at Knipp's singing. He cleared all his money matters to his complete satisfaction, spied young Mrs. Daniel and Sarah in town and shyly dogged them without finding them again. He dined merrily with Sir W. Warren, Mr. Hinton and others, then went home by water over a river full of ice, a little frightened. That evening he played cards and supped with Mrs. Tooker, Mrs. Daniel and Sarah, until Mr. Pierce told him W. Howe had used his name to send goods under Lord Bruncker's seal, which vexed him mightily, though he held back his discontent until he could speak with Lord Bruncker. He returned to cards late, having great pleasure with Mrs. Tooker.

He dined merrily at Captain Cocke's, visited the Exchange to find his pretty seamstress and was mightily joyed to see her, then handled money for Lord Sandwich in Lumbard Street. That night he supped merrily with Mrs. Penington, asked her to undress for a picture, walked out in the dark frosty night and found her gone to bed. At home he kissed young Mrs. Daniel while she asked him to help her husband become a Lieutenant, then went to bed pleased about his money. Two things trouble him: the sickness increased above 80 this week, and his accounts for Tangier and other dealings are so complex that he has not made them even with himself for 3 or 4 months.
